title: Handling complaints
blurb: What the GDC expects, how to respond calmly at the front line, practice procedure and timescales, and where NHS and private patients can go next.
question: A patient comes back to reception, upset and raising her voice, because her new crown feels wrong and she was kept waiting 40 minutes last time. She says she wants to 'make a formal complaint'. What should you do in the moment, and what happens next?

teach.body: GDC Principle 5 says every practice must have a clear and effective complaints procedure. Patients have a right to complain, and a complaint handled well often ends with a patient who trusts the practice more. Handled badly, it can escalate to the NHS, an ombudsman, the Dental Complaints Service or the GDC. Every member of the team should know the procedure, where it is displayed, and who the complaints lead is.

steps.label: Stay calm
steps.sub: Move somewhere private if you can

steps.label: Note the facts
steps.sub: What happened, when, what they want

steps.label: Explain next steps
steps.sub: Pass it to the complaints lead; give them the procedure

teach.caption: Your aim is to help the patient feel heard and to pass the complaint on accurately, not to defend or decide.

teach.h: Saying sorry is not admitting fault
teach.body: Saying you are sorry that the patient is upset, or sorry for their experience, is kind and professional. It is not an admission of negligence. What you must not do is argue, blame a colleague, make promises you can't keep (such as a refund) or discuss the complaint with others who don't need to know. If the patient is abusive or threatening, stay safe and get a senior colleague.

items.label: working days to acknowledge a complaint (GDC)
working days to aim for a full response (GDC)
months: usual time limit to make an NHS complaint

teach.caption: If a full response will take longer, keep the patient updated and explain why. The response should address every point raised and say what they can do if they are still unhappy.

teach.h: If the practice can't resolve it

children.label: Commissioner
children.sub: ICB in England, then the Ombudsman

teach.caption: NHS patients can complain to the practice or to the commissioner first. The Ombudsman (the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman in England) reviews unresolved NHS complaints. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own NHS routes and ombudsmen.

teach.text: The Dental Complaints Service handles complaints about PRIVATE dental care only. NHS complaints go to the practice or commissioner, then the Ombudsman. The GDC deals with serious concerns about a registrant's fitness to practise, not everyday service complaints.

teach.h: NHS and private complaints side by side

teach.body: Every complaint should be recorded in a complaints log, kept separate from the patient's clinical record so it doesn't affect their future care. The practice reviews complaints for patterns, shares lessons with the team (anonymised) and changes how it works. Complaints handling is a GDC recommended CPD topic. If a complaint is about your own care, reflect on it honestly and tell your indemnity provider if it may become a claim.

items: GDC Principle 5: every practice needs a clear and effective complaints procedure.
Stay calm, listen, acknowledge, note the facts and follow the procedure.
Apologising for the patient's experience is not an admission of liability.
GDC: acknowledge within 3 working days; aim to respond fully within 10 working days.
Unresolved: NHS to the commissioner and Ombudsman; private to the Dental Complaints Service.

summary: You can now respond calmly to an upset patient, take and pass on a complaint correctly, explain the GDC's expectations and timescales, and direct patients to the right next step: the commissioner and Ombudsman for NHS care, the Dental Complaints Service for private care, and the GDC for fitness to practise concerns.

A.q: A patient arrives at reception angry about a long delay at his last visit. What is the best first action?
options: Explain that the dentist had an emergency that day
Listen calmly and acknowledge his frustration
Ask him to put his concerns in writing first
Offer a discount on his next appointment
A.why: Listening and acknowledging his feelings calms the situation and shows him he has been heard, before anything else happens.

whyNot.0: Jumping to explanations can sound defensive before he has finished speaking.
whyNot.2: Complaints can be made verbally; insisting on writing first can feel dismissive.
whyNot.3: Offering money is not your decision to make and doesn't address the complaint.

A.q: Under GDC standards, what must every dental practice have?
options: A complaints insurance policy
An in-house complaints solicitor
A clear and effective complaints procedure
A rule that complaints are made in writing
A.why: GDC Principle 5 requires a clear and effective complaints procedure that patients can easily find and use.

whyNot.0: Indemnity covers claims, but the GDC standard is about having a complaints procedure.
whyNot.1: There is no requirement for a solicitor; the practice handles complaints through its procedure.
whyNot.3: Patients may complain verbally or in writing; both must be accepted.

A.q: A private patient is unhappy with the practice's final response to her complaint. Where can she go next?
options: The Health Service Ombudsman
The Care Quality Commission
The local Integrated Care Board
The Dental Complaints Service
A.why: The Dental Complaints Service is a free, impartial service for complaints about private dental care.

whyNot.0: The Health Service Ombudsman reviews NHS complaints, not private ones.
whyNot.1: The CQC regulates and inspects services but does not resolve individual complaints.
whyNot.2: ICBs commission NHS dentistry, so they deal with NHS complaints only.

B.q: A patient complains to you about a colleague's manner. What is the most appropriate immediate response?
options: Agree that the colleague can be abrupt at times
Listen, apologise and follow the procedure
Defend your colleague's usually good manner
Say complaints like this rarely change anything
B.why: Listening, apologising for their experience and following the procedure is professional and fair to everyone involved.

whyNot.0: Criticising a colleague to a patient is unprofessional and prejudges the complaint.
whyNot.2: Defending the colleague dismisses the patient's experience before it has been looked into.
whyNot.3: This discourages the patient and goes against the purpose of a complaints procedure.

B.q: According to GDC guidance, how quickly should a practice acknowledge a complaint?
options: Within 3 working days
Within 24 hours
Within 28 days
Within 10 working days
B.why: The GDC expects complaints to be acknowledged within three working days, with a full response aimed for within ten.

whyNot.1: A quick reply is good practice, but the GDC standard is three working days.
whyNot.2: 28 days is far too long to leave a complaint unacknowledged.
whyNot.3: Ten working days is the target for a full response, not the acknowledgement.

B.q: An NHS patient remains unhappy after the practice and commissioner have responded. Who can review the complaint independently?
options: The Dental Complaints Service
The British Dental Association
The Health Service Ombudsman
The practice's indemnity provider
B.why: The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman makes final, independent decisions on unresolved NHS complaints in England.

whyNot.0: The Dental Complaints Service deals with private dental care only.
whyNot.1: The BDA is a professional association for dentists, not a complaints body.
whyNot.3: Indemnity providers support professionals; they don't review complaints independently.

C.q: A patient raises his voice in the surgery about his treatment. What is the most appropriate initial response?
options: Raise your own voice so he can hear you
Ask him to leave the surgery until he has calmed down
Tell him the dentist did nothing wrong at all
Stay calm, listen and acknowledge his concern
C.why: Remaining calm and listening helps de-escalate the situation and shows him his concern is being taken seriously.

whyNot.0: Matching his volume escalates the conflict.
whyNot.1: Asking him to leave straight away may inflame things; listening comes first unless anyone is unsafe.
whyNot.2: Defending the dentist before hearing him out sounds dismissive and prejudges the complaint.

C.q: Where should details of a patient's complaint be recorded?
options: In a complaints log, separate from clinical notes
In the patient's clinical record, under 'Notes'
In the daily appointment book, beside the visit
Nowhere, provided it is resolved on the same day
C.why: Complaints are recorded in a separate log so they can be reviewed for learning without affecting the patient's clinical record or future care.

whyNot.1: Putting complaints in the clinical record could affect how the patient is treated in future.
whyNot.2: The appointment book is not secure or suitable for complaint details.
whyNot.3: Even complaints resolved on the day should be recorded so the practice can learn from them.

C.q: Which statement about apologising to a complainant is correct?
options: It legally admits the practice was negligent
Only the practice owner is allowed to apologise
It can be given without admitting liability
It should wait until the investigation ends
C.why: Saying sorry for the patient's experience is professional and compassionate, and does not in itself admit liability.

whyNot.0: An apology is not, of itself, an admission of negligence.
whyNot.1: Any team member can apologise that a patient is upset or has had a poor experience.
whyNot.3: Waiting can make the patient feel ignored; a sincere early apology often helps.

reteach.title: Think of a complaint as a relay race
reteach.question: Picture a baton passing from runner to runner. Where does the front-line team member's leg of the race start and finish?

blocks.h: Your leg: receive it well, pass it cleanly
blocks.body: You don't have to win the whole race. Your leg is to receive the complaint well (stay calm, listen, acknowledge, apologise for their experience) and pass it cleanly to the complaints lead with accurate notes. The practice runs the next leg: acknowledge in 3 working days, aim for a full answer in 10. If the patient still isn't satisfied, the baton goes outside the practice: commissioner and Ombudsman for NHS care, the Dental Complaints Service for private care.

items.label: Outside route: ICB / Ombudsman or DCS

blocks.text: Dropping the baton: arguing, blaming a colleague or promising a refund all make things worse. Stick to listening, acknowledging and following the procedure.

explain.body: Stay calm, move somewhere private if possible, listen without interrupting, acknowledge their feelings, note the facts and explain what happens next. Don't argue, blame or promise outcomes.

test.q: An upset patient is complaining loudly in a busy waiting room. What should you do first?
options: Ask them to lower their voice or leave
Explain the complaints policy word for word
Invite them somewhere private to talk
Tell them to email the practice manager
test.why: Moving somewhere private protects their confidentiality and dignity, and makes it easier to listen and calm things down.

whyNot.0: This can escalate things before you have listened.
whyNot.1: Reading out the policy before listening feels cold and dismissive.
whyNot.3: Sending them away to email can feel like being brushed off.

explain.body: The complaints lead acknowledges the complaint within 3 working days and aims for a full written response within 10 working days, addressing every point and saying what the patient can do if still unhappy. If it will take longer, the patient is kept updated.

test.q: What should a full response to a complaint include?
options: Only the outcome of the investigation
A reply to every point and next steps
A request to withdraw the complaint
Copies of the dentist's private notes
test.why: A good response deals with every issue raised and tells the patient where to go if they remain dissatisfied.

whyNot.0: An outcome without addressing each point leaves the patient feeling unheard.
whyNot.2: Asking a patient to withdraw a complaint is inappropriate.
whyNot.3: The response should explain findings, not hand over internal notes.

explain.body: NHS: complain to the practice or the commissioner (ICB in England), then the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman. Private: the Dental Complaints Service. Serious concerns about a professional's fitness to practise: the GDC.

test.q: Which body handles complaints about private dental care that the practice could not resolve?
options: The Dental Complaints Service
The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
The Integrated Care Board
NHS Resolution
test.why: The Dental Complaints Service is a free, impartial service for private dental complaints.

whyNot.2: ICBs handle complaints about NHS services they commission.
whyNot.3: NHS Resolution deals with NHS clinical negligence claims, not private complaints.
